To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the methane emissions of individual adult Merino ewes confined in respiration systems are related to the amount of feed they eat on the day of measurement and the two previous ones, but are unaffected by their sire or liveweight.
methane yield of sheep in RC is influenced by feed intake on the previous 2 days and that sire effects on methane yield are confounded with feed intake.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of genetic markers for low methane emissions and the identification of genetic markers for feed intake in sheep.
the development of a model that can be used to predict methane emissions in the field, using information on feed intake and LW.
the development of a genetic evaluation for methane emissions in sheep.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a genetic component to variation in methane yield in sheep, which can be detected in respiration chambers, but that the effect is small and may be masked by confounding factors.
there is no evidence for genetic variation in methane emissions in sheep.
methane emissions of sheep can be affected by sires, but only after the effects of feed intake on previous and current days have been removed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
methane production is related to feed intake and that the genetic variation in methane production is small.

the variation in methane yield between sires, which was not significant before correcting for confounding factors, was not significantly different from zero after correcting for feed intake in RC and the previous 2 days.

the variation between sires for methane emissions in the 1st RC test is due largely to variation in feed intake, and that variation between sires is not evident in feed intake, but is in methane production, when the confounding effects of feed intake are taken into account.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a large variation between sires for feed intake and methane yield in sheep.
methane emissions of individual sheep are highly variable, but that variation is largely explained by variation in feed eaten on previous days.
the genetic variation in methane emissions is small, and the heritability is probably close to zero, because of confounding factors.
